title: Mikhail Baryshnikov
wiki_lead:
Mikhail Nikolayevich Baryshnikov (born January 27, 1948) is a Latvian and American dancer, choreographer, and actor. He was the preeminent male classical ballet dancer of the 1970s and 1980s. He subsequently became a noted dance director.
Born into a Russian family in Riga, Latvian SSR, Soviet Union, Baryshnikov had a promising start in the Kirov Ballet before defecting to Canada in 1974 for more opportunities in Western dance. After dancing with the American Ballet Theatre, he joined the New York City Ballet as a principal dancer for one season to learn about George Balanchine's neoclassical Russian style of movement. Baryshnikov then returned to the American Ballet Theatre, where he later became artistic director. He has spearheaded many of his own artistic projects and has been associated in particular with promoting modern dance, premiering dozens of new works, including many of his own.
Baryshnikov's success as a dramatic actor on stage, cinema, and television has helped him become probably the most widely recognized contemporary ballet dancer. He starred in the films The Turning Point (1977)—for which he received nominations for an Academy Award and a Golden Globe Award—and White Nights (1985), and had a recurring role in the last season of the television series Sex and the City.
Baryshnikov never returned to the Soviet Union after his defection. He has been a naturalized citizen of the United States since 1986. He often returned to Latvia after the country declared independence in 1990. In 2017, Latvia granted him citizenship for extraordinary merit.

Early life
Mikhail Nikolayevich Baryshnikov was born into a family of ethnic Russians in Riga, then the capital of the Latvian SSR, Soviet Union. His mother, Alexandra (née Kiselyova), was a dressmaker, and his father, Nikolay Baryshnikov, was an engineer. According to Baryshnikov, his father was a strict and nationalist military man, while his mother introduced him to theatre, opera, and ballet. She died by suicide when Baryshnikov was 12 years old.


Dancing career


1960–1974: Early years
Baryshnikov began his ballet studies in Riga at the age of nine. He entered the Vaganova School in 1964. Baryshnikov soon won the top prize in the junior division of the Varna International Ballet Competition. He joined the Mariinsky Ballet, then called the Kirov Ballet, in 1967, dancing the "Peasant" pas de deux in Giselle. Recognizing Baryshnikov's talent, particularly his stage presence and purity of technique, several Soviet choreographers, including Oleg Vinogradov, Konstantin Sergeyev, Igor Tchernichov, and Leonid Jakobson, choreographed ballets for him. Baryshnikov made signature roles of Jakobson's 1969 virtuosic Vestris along with an intensely emotional Albrecht in Giselle. While he was still in the Soviet Union, New York Times critic Clive Barnes called him "the most perfect dancer I have ever seen."


1974: Defection to Canada
Baryshnikov's talent was obvious from his youth, but being 5 ft 5 in or 5 ft 6 in (165 or 168 cm) tall—shorter than most male ballet dancers—he could not tower over a ballerina en pointe and was therefore relegated to secondary parts. More frustrating to him, the Soviet dance world hewed closely to 19th-century traditions and deliberately shunned Western choreographers, whose work Baryshnikov glimpsed in occasional tours and films. His main reason for leaving the Soviet Union was to work with these innovators.
On June 29, 1974, in Toronto while on tour with the Bolshoi, Baryshnikov defected, requesting political asylum in Canada. As recalled by John Fraser, a ballet critic from Toronto who helped Baryshnikov to escape, Fraser wrote down phone numbers of people on a small piece of paper and hid it under his wedding ring. grok_lead: Mikhail Nikolayevich Baryshnikov (born January 27, 1948) is a Latvian-born dancer, choreographer, and actor renowned for his virtuosic technique and artistry in classical ballet. After training at the Vaganova Academy and rising to principal dancer with the Kirov Ballet in Leningrad, he defected from the Soviet Union on June 29, 1974, during a tour in Toronto, Canada, seeking political asylum to pursue artistic freedom unavailable under communist restrictions. In the West, Baryshnikov joined the American Ballet Theatre as a principal dancer, later serving as its artistic director from 1980 to 1990, where he championed innovative choreography and repertory expansion. He co-founded the White Oak Dance Project in 1990 with choreographer Mark Morris, touring contemporary works until 2002, and has received prestigious honors including the Kennedy Center Honors and the National Medal of Arts for his contributions to dance. Baryshnikov extended his career into acting, earning an Academy Award nomination for The Turning Point (1977) and multiple Emmy Awards for television performances, while establishing the Baryshnikov Arts Center in New York to support interdisciplinary artists. A naturalized U.S. citizen who later acquired Latvian citizenship, his defection symbolized individual defiance against Soviet cultural control, influencing generations of performers.
